summary: Describes an experiment in which addresses and names are derived from geographic position, using specific example addresses and domain names. It is an experimental proposal, not a standard.

eli5.summary: Your house's address would be its exact spot on the globe, like a pin on a map. This note tries out that idea.

questions: how does location based routing work
subtitle: Routing IP packets based on geographic location instead of IP addresses

tldr.problem: The Internet routes packets using logical IP addresses, but mobile and location-aware applications need to send messages to geographic areas rather than fixed hosts or networks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2009 proposes two routing schemes: a multicast-based approach that maps geographic regions to multicast groups, and a geometric routing approach that uses polygon intersection to determine packet forwarding.
tldr.outcome: The RFC was published as an experimental exploration of location-based networking, but geographic routing was never standardized or implemented in the Internet, and location services evolved using different approaches.

today: RFC 2009 remains an Experimental RFC from November 1996 and was never standardized or deployed in the Internet. Geographic routing concepts were interesting but impractical at the time, and location-aware services evolved differently, using application-layer approaches, DNS extensions, and eventually commercial GPS and cellular-based location services. The RFC's ideas about hierarchical geographic partitioning and polygon-based addressing influenced later research but did not result in operational protocols.

sections.title: GPS-Based Addressing
sections.content:
RFC 2009 proposes methods to integrate GPS (Global Positioning System) location data into Internet routing and addressing. Instead of sending a message to an IP address like 192.0.2.1, applications could send a message to a geographic location like 'everyone within a 2-mile radius of latitude 40.5, longitude -74.0'. This enables location-dependent services such as flood warnings sent to residents near a river, emergency broadcasts in specific areas, or location-based directory services.

The RFC assumes a cellular architecture with Mobile Support Stations (MSS) that serve geographic cells with well-defined coverage areas. It proposes using GPS coordinates as addresses, represented either as polygons (latitude/longitude point sequences) or simple shapes (circles) that describe the target region. An eight-byte GPS address can specify locations with precision down to 0.1 mile.
sections.eli5: Instead of saying 'send to 192.0.2.1', you say 'send to everyone in this map area'. The router looks at the GPS coordinates and delivers it to all the cells that overlap that area.

sections.title: Geographic Addressing Model
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a hierarchical addressing scheme using two-dimensional GPS coordinates (latitude and longitude). Addresses can specify specific locations by polygon (a list of connected GPS points), by circle (center point and radius), or by postal-like names (city_hall.Fresno.California.USA) resolved through DNS.

Geographic regions are divided into atoms (smallest addressable areas, around the size of a cell) and partitions (larger areas like counties or states). This hierarchy allows scalability: routers in New Jersey need only know about large partitions covering California, not every individual cell. The addressing space is flexible—with IPv6's larger address space, atoms could be much smaller.
sections.eli5: Geography is like a pyramid: your house is in a city, which is in a county, which is in a state. Routers far away only know about big territories; local routers know the details.

sections.title: GPS-Multicast Routing Scheme (GPSM)
sections.content:
The first routing solution uses multicast. Each geographic partition and atom is mapped to an IP multicast address using a hierarchical format: 1111.GPS.S.C.x, where GPS is a 6-bit code reserving 1/64 of the multicast space, S encodes the state, C encodes the county within the state, and x encodes atoms within the county.

Each Mobile Support Station joins multicast groups for all partitions that intersect its radio cell's coverage area. When a sender wants to send to a geographic polygon, it approximates the polygon with the smallest partition containing it, sends the packet with that partition's multicast address, and includes the precise polygon in the packet body. The multicast routing delivers the packet to all base stations in the partition, which then filter on the application layer using the exact polygon coordinates.
sections.eli5: You send to 'the New York state group'. All New York base stations get it. They look at the polygon in the packet and only send it to cells that overlap that exact area.

sections.title: Geometric Routing Scheme (GEO)
sections.content:
The second solution uses pure geometric routing with a hierarchy of GPS routers. Routers are arranged by geographic scope: country routers at the top, state routers below them, city routers below that, and base station routers at the bottom. Each router knows its service area (the union of all its children's service areas) as a polygon.

When a GPScast message arrives at a router, the router computes the intersection between the destination polygon and its service area polygon. If they don't overlap, it forwards the message up to its parent router. If they do overlap, the router subtracts its service area from the destination polygon and sends the remainder to its parent, while forwarding the intersection portion to child base stations that serve that area. This algorithm efficiently routes messages through multiple levels of hierarchy.
sections.eli5: Each router has a map of what area it covers. When a message arrives, it checks if any of its cells are in the destination area. If so, it sends to those cells. If the destination extends beyond its area, it sends the rest upstairs.

sections.title: Implementation Details and Supporting Protocols
sections.content:
RFC 2009 defines several supporting components. SendToGPS() and RecvFromGPS() library functions provide the application interface. GPSRouteD is the router daemon that implements the routing logic, using tunnels to connect GPS routers over the existing IP network.

The Internet GPS Management Protocol (IGPSMP) allows routers to report their service areas to parent and peer routers using messages like 'service area query', 'service area report', and 'alive signal' to detect failures. The Multicast Address Resolution Protocol (MARP) helps mobile hosts discover which multicast address to join for their current cell. Routers cache recently-seen GPScast packets to reduce geometric computation overhead for streams like audio or video.
sections.eli5: These are the helper protocols: how routers tell each other what areas they cover, how mobile phones find their cell's multicast group, and how routers remember where they just sent a message.

layers.label: Country Routers
layers.detail: Route between geographical regions, each manages multiple state routers

layers.label: State Routers
layers.detail: Each covers a state or large region, manages city routers

layers.label: City Routers
layers.detail: Each covers a city or metropolitan area, manages base station routers

layers.label: Base Station Routers
layers.detail: Serve individual cells, deliver messages to mobile hosts via wireless

left.title: Multicast Scheme (GPSM)
left.desc: Maps polygons to multicast groups; routers join groups for their cell's partitions. Simpler but requires application-level filtering.

right.title: Geometric Scheme (GEO)
right.desc: Uses polygon intersection at each router level; routers determine exactly which sub-areas to reach. More complex but pure IP layer.
